text: Slot reservation agreements for our heavy-duty frames now run into 2029, and we are asking customers for larger deposits to hold a place in the queue. Pricing on new heavy-duty gas orders continued to step up this quarter.

Our ability to bring new capacity online in several regions is limited less by chips than by how quickly we can get megawatts delivered to the site. We expect to remain short of capacity through at least the end of the fiscal year.

A year ago energization dates were the gating item on most of our builds; today, with the additional generation and substation work we contracted coming in, that is no longer what sets the schedule. We now have line of sight to the electricity we need for next year's campus openings.

Several utilities trimmed their large-load forecasts this month after developers withdrew speculative hyperscale requests, freeing up headroom that had been booked years in advance. Grid planners said the number of pending data center connection requests in the region fell by nearly a quarter since spring.

We may enter into long-term power purchase arrangements with technology companies co-located at or near our generating facilities. The terms, timing and regulatory treatment of any such arrangements are uncertain and may not be approved as proposed.

Our service territory includes one of the largest concentrations of data center load in the world, and we serve these customers under a separate rate class. We plan transmission and generation investments through our integrated resource planning process filed with state regulators.

Our stacked-die output for next calendar year is fully committed on both volume and price, and we continue to see customer demand that exceeds what we can ship. Bit supply for conventional server parts is also tight because wafer starts have shifted toward the stacked products.

Contract prices for server DRAM modules rose for a third straight quarter, according to market trackers, as module makers scrambled for allocation. Some OEMs reported receiving only 70 percent of requested volumes.

Gross margin benefited from a more favorable commodity environment, as the cost of the memory content in our servers declined sequentially. We expect those input costs to stay benign into next quarter.

Spot quotes for mainstream DRAM chips slipped again this week as distributors sat on bloated stockpiles and PC builders delayed orders. Analysts said the inventory overhang could take two quarters to clear.

The semiconductor memory and storage markets are highly competitive and have historically been characterized by periods of significant oversupply and undersupply. Changes in industry capacity, technology transitions and customer inventory levels could adversely affect our average selling prices.

We rely on a limited number of suppliers for certain components of our servers, including high-bandwidth memory used in our accelerators. Any disruption to these suppliers could delay our infrastructure plans.

Orders grew faster than sales again, taking backlog to a new high, with thermal products leading. We are adding shifts at our coolant distribution unit lines and still quoting delivery windows several months longer than customers want.

Rack builders say a shortage of drip-free quick-disconnect couplings and cold plates is holding up shipments of their densest systems. One integrator described the fittings as the hardest part on the bill of materials to source this year.

With the new facility now at full rate, our lead times on chillers and air handlers for data center customers are back to where they were before the surge. We have the capacity to take on additional programs without extending delivery dates.

Earlier in the year, delays in the delivery of the heat-rejection equipment for our direct-to-chip halls pushed out a couple of go-live dates. Those deliveries are now arriving on plan, and we don't expect cooling equipment to constrain our deployments next year.

Our building solutions segment designs, manufactures and services HVAC equipment, including centrifugal chillers used in mission-critical facilities such as data centers. We sell through direct channels and independent distributors.

Industry analysts describe a market split between rear-door heat exchangers, direct liquid loops and immersion tanks, with no single approach yet dominant. Operators are evaluating options as rack power densities rise.

Demand for our 800-gig and 1.6-terabit transceivers continues to run ahead of our indium phosphide laser capacity. We are doubling six-inch wafer output, but expect to remain supply-constrained for the next several quarters.

Hyperscale customers have signed multi-year agreements that commit a significant portion of our glass draw capacity, and we are running our plants flat out. We raised prices on several connectivity products to reflect the tightness.
Component lead times have normalized, and we were able to reduce our purchase commitments for the second consecutive quarter. Our switch delivery times are now back to standard.

Prices for 400G pluggable optics have dropped sharply as Asian module makers brought new lines online, according to a supply-chain research firm. Buyers that were rationed last year are now receiving full orders.

We depend on third parties for components of our technical infrastructure, including optical interconnects and switching hardware. If these suppliers fail to deliver, our ability to expand our data centers could be harmed.
We provide coherent optical transport systems, pluggable modules and routing platforms to service providers, cloud operators and enterprises. Our products move data between and within data centers.

Concentrate markets are as tight as we have seen, with smelter treatment charges falling below zero in some spot deals. Refined copper demand from electrical infrastructure and data centers is outpacing new mine supply.

Physical premiums for copper cathode delivered to U.S. buyers hit a record this week as warehouse stocks dwindled. Wire and cable makers reported difficulty securing metal for first-quarter production.

We supply high-purity nitrogen, argon and specialty process gases to semiconductor fabs, typically under long-term on-site contracts with take-or-pay provisions. These contracts generally include pass-through of energy costs.
Helium markets remained oversupplied, and pricing declined as new sources came online. We expect continued pressure on helium volumes and price over the coming year.
Copper fell to a six-month low as Chinese buyers stepped back and exchange inventories climbed for a fifth week. Traders said the supply deficit forecast earlier in the year now looks overstated.
We purchase significant quantities of copper, steel and aluminum. Volatility in the prices of these raw materials could affect our margins if we are unable to pass increases through to customers.

Utilities are waiting three to four years for the large units that step voltage down at substations, and some are buying refurbished equipment to fill the gap. Industry groups warned the shortage could delay new housing developments and factory hookups.

Backlog in Electrical Americas grew again to a record level, and book-to-bill remained above one. Demand for switchgear and medium-voltage equipment continues to exceed our capacity even as new plants ramp.
Utility customers worked down the inventory they built during the shortage period, which weighed on distribution orders. Our lead times on pole-mount units have come back to pre-pandemic levels.

Three new transformer factories opened in the Southeast this year, and buyers say quoted delivery times for pad-mounted units have shortened by several months. Prices have stabilized after two years of steep increases.

We procure major electrical equipment, including transformers and circuit breakers, from a limited number of manufacturers, some located outside the United States. Supply disruptions, tariffs or trade restrictions could increase our costs or delay projects.

We design and manufacture custom-engineered equipment that distributes, controls and monitors electrical energy, including metal-clad switchgear and integrated power control rooms. Our customers include utilities, oil and gas producers and commercial and industrial users.

Lithium pricing remained under pressure through the quarter as new supply from Africa and South America continued to outstrip demand. In response, we are idling some conversion capacity and deferring expansion projects.
Battery-grade carbonate prices slid to a fresh low as producers kept output high despite swelling inventories at cathode makers. Analysts expect the glut to persist into next year.

Since the new export licensing rules took effect, we have seen tighter availability of anode-grade graphite and longer shipment times from some suppliers. We are qualifying alternate sources, but this is a constraint on cell output in the near term.

Cobalt prices surged after the Democratic Republic of Congo extended its export quotas, leaving refiners racing to secure feedstock. Some cathode producers said they were operating on weeks of supply.

We have entered into offtake agreements and equity investments with several lithium and nickel producers to support our battery cell production. These arrangements are subject to project development risks and may not deliver the expected volumes.
Our base metals business produces nickel products sold to stainless steel and battery precursor customers. We operate mines and refineries in Canada, Brazil and Indonesia.

Distributors have finished working down the stock they accumulated during the shortages, and our product lead times are now back to normal across most of the portfolio. We have ample capacity to support a demand recovery.

Factory orders for electric motors and variable-speed drives fell for a second month, according to an industry trade group, as manufacturers postponed upgrades. Discounting has returned in the distribution channel.
Orders outpaced shipments again, and we placed certain larger motor frames on allocation for the remainder of the year. We implemented a second price increase to offset higher magnet and steel costs.

A squeeze on rare-earth magnet supply is forcing some motor manufacturers to slow production lines, according to people familiar with the matter. Several automation equipment makers warned customers of longer delivery times.
Our motion and control technologies include electromechanical actuators, servo drives and controllers sold to industrial OEMs and through distribution. We serve a broad range of end markets.

We continue to invest in automating our hub network, including robotic sorting and conveyor systems. We expect a majority of our volume to flow through automated facilities over the next several years.
